Does query ORDER influence output? Yes for DRC and geometry, no for connectivity and zone-fill queries:
- ORDER-SENSITIVE: (1) drc_test_provider_copper_clearance.cpp:704-708 stops after the first violation per track/layer unless --all-track-errors (default false, drc_engine.cpp:94), so which violation is reported follows tree order; (2) drc_rtree.h:391-443 QueryColliding keeps `curActual < actual` and stops at actual<=0, so the marker position of an overlapping item/zone is the first intersecting triangle in tree order; (3) copper_clearance.cpp:1337-1373 testZonesToZones reports pt/otherPt/actual of the first segment pair under clearance; (4) shape_poly_tri_index.h:182-196 AnyTriangleHit (strict `<`, first tie wins) feeds SHAPE_POLY_SET::Collide(...,&actual,&location); (5) shape_poly_set.cpp:2483-2507 splitSelfTouchingOutlines takes the first pinch candidate; (6) DRC_RTREE::OnLayer iterates in packed order (QueryCollidingPairs).
- NORMALISED by KiCad itself (any order works): zone_filler.cpp:404-428 (sorted by board sequence), drc_zone_index.h:87,150 (sorted), shape_collisions.cpp:575-577 ("Candidate IDs restore the legacy order").
- ORDER-INSENSITIVE: connectivity (CN_VISITOR always returns true, CN_ITEM::Connect inserts with lower_bound, deferred net codes are sorted: connectivity_algo.cpp:310-378), and all boolean queries.
The packed order = Hilbert key order, and ties (identical bbox centres: pad+hole, via on pad, the two triangles of a rectangle) are resolved by libstdc++'s unstable std::sort.

candidates.notes: R*-tree, 28 releases 2018-11..2026-11 (georust), deps heapless/num-traits/ordered-float/smallvec, MSRV 1.90 (workspace rust-version 1.85 + resolver 3 locks 0.13.1). Has bulk_load, insert, remove, locate_in_envelope_intersecting (closed intervals, same predicate as KiCad), 2D and 3D. Result SETS equal KIRTREE in 100% of 20,850 queries (bulk/insert/remove, 2D+3D, f64 coords) but ORDER equals PACKED_RTREE in only 438 of 6,927 multi-hit queries (first hit equal in 822). Integer coordinates are unsafe with overflow checks: AABB<[i32;2]> panics on insert at nm scale (area = product in the scalar type); i64 panics for boxes spanning the i32 range and for {layer,x,y}; f64 or Wrapping<i64> work.

Sets equal in 10,900/10,900 queries; order equal in 435/6,927 multi-hit queries (16-bit Hilbert grid, different node layout and tie order). With i32 coordinates it panics (subtract overflow in build) on 38/40 full-int-range cases; fine with f64.

libs.recommendation: port by hand (kicad-geom): PACKED_RTREE exactly, DYNAMIC_RTREE exactly (or at least BulkLoad+Search), COW_RTREE only if Tier 3; no external crate.
libs.rationale: No crate can reproduce KIRTREE's visit order, and DRC output (which violation, marker position, actual distance) depends on it. A statement-by-statement port does reproduce it bit for bit, provided the Hilbert sort and the R*-tree split/reinsert sorts use a port of libstdc++'s std::sort (see the std::sort entry). Working prototypes exist and can be lifted: /home/user/kicad-source-mirror/rust/target/research/spatial/src/packed_rtree.rs (315 lines) and src/dynamic_rtree.rs (1151 lines, arena-based, no unsafe). Porting notes found the hard way: HilbertXY2D needs wrapping u32 arithmetic (`s*2-1-x` wraps for s=2^31); DYNAMIC_RTREE area/overlap products overflow int64 for whole-range boxes (UB in C++, wraps in practice) so use wrapping_mul; the SSE2/NEON OverlapMask2D paths are the same closed-interval predicate as the scalar one. For CN_RTREE alone any exact AABB index would do (order-insensitive); rstar with f64 is a verified fallback but adds nothing over the hand port.
libs.fidelity_risk: low with the hand port (visit order verified identical to g++/libstdc++ on every query tested; residual risk is that the tie order is libstdc++-specific, i.e. the port matches a Linux/GCC oracle, not MSVC/libc++ builds of KiCad). HIGH if a crate is substituted: 91-94% of multi-hit queries come back in a different order, which changes first-hit DRC results.

- Hand port DynamicRTree: visit order identical 20,850/20,850 for each of BulkLoad, Insert, Remove (2D+3D), same on 2 more seeds (187,650 query comparisons), including the full-int-range cases where int64 wraps.
- All C++ trees agree with brute force as sets (sanity).
- Crates: numbers in the candidate notes; overflow panics reproduced with overflow-checks on (src/bin/rstar_int.rs, rtree_cmp).
- wasm32-unknown-unknown: whole scratch project builds; checksums over all visit orders computed inside WebAssembly (node 22) equal the native ones for both ports.

libs.kicad_usage: One user: pcbnew/ratsnest/ratsnest_data.cpp:47,228 (RN_NET::TRIANGULATOR_STATE::Triangulate; library linked into pcbcommon, common/CMakeLists.txt:1332). Input contract: >= 3 anchors with unique integer nm positions sorted by x then y (CN_PTR_CMP), not all exactly collinear (areNodesColinear handles that case). Uses only `triangles` and `halfedges`: every undirected edge becomes an MST candidate; kruskalMST then runs with a strict total order (weight, endpoints, tags), so triangle ORDER is irrelevant but the SET of edges matters. The MST edges are the ratsnest, i.e. what DRC reports as unconnected items (Tier 1 connectivity + unconnected test).

libs.recommendation: port by hand (statement-by-statement port of delaunator.cpp, ~620 lines of Rust, in kicad-connectivity or kicad-geom) together with the libstdc++ std::sort port.
libs.rationale: The hand port is byte-identical to the bundled C++ on every case tried, including the cases where the C++ produces an incomplete triangulation, so the ratsnest is reproduced exactly. The crate is a different algorithm variant. Its differing diagonals on cocircular (grid) sets turned out not to change KiCad's MST (0 MST differences in all grid/cocircular/random categories, also with random pre-connected pairs - consistent with the fact that an interior chord of a cocircular polygon is always the strictly longest edge of one adjacent triangle), but on near-collinear anchor sets (a pad row a few nm off a line, e.g. rotated footprints) the MST differs: 57/284 board-scale near-collinear sets, 1/146 rotated pad rows, 1/394 tiny integer sets. Prototype: /home/user/kicad-source-mirror/rust/target/research/spatial/src/delaunator_port.rs. Porting notes: do size_t index maths in u64 so wasm32 matches (INVALID_INDEX, hash_key); hash_key must map NaN (point exactly at the circumcentre) to 2^63 like glibc llround; keep the exact floating expression order (x86-64 GCC does not contract to FMA); the C++ `throw`/assert paths become errors.
libs.fidelity_risk: low with the hand port (bit-identical triangles/halfedges/hull; depends on the libstdc++ sort tie order like the oracle). medium if the `delaunator` crate is used: identical ratsnest on well-conditioned and gridded nets, different on near-collinear nets. Note a KiCad quirk the port will faithfully reproduce: the bundled C++ leaves anchors out of the triangulation on 142 of 2,721 test sets (all near-collinear), which yields missing ratsnest edges.
libs.experiments:
cpp/delaunator_driver.cpp built with g++ 13.3 -O2 against thirdparty/delaunator; src/bin/delaunay_cmp.rs generates point sets and compares triangles, halfedges, hull, undirected edge set and the KiCad-style Kruskal MST. - Hand port vs C++: output files byte-identical (cmp) for all 3,050 cases, and for 14 further seeds: 37,096 cases in total; the 29 all-collinear cases fail identically (C++ throws "not triangulation").
- Crate 1.1.0 vs C++: figures in the candidate notes; MST differs in 125/2,721 contract cases (all in near-collinear categories, plus the two singletons above).
- wasm32: delaunator crate and the port build; a checksum over triangles/halfedges/hull of all 3,050 cases computed in WebAssembly (node 22) equals the native value.

libs.recommendation: port by hand: the ~400-line subset of nanoflann KiCad uses (divideTree/middleSplit_/planeSplit, searchLevel, KNNResultSet, RadiusResultSet). A brute-force scan is an acceptable simplification for the radius query only.
libs.rationale: Point counts are tiny (outline end points) so performance is irrelevant; what matters is (a) the strict `<` radius boundary on f64 squared distances, which every candidate gets right with care, and (b) the order of equidistant neighbours in knnSearch, which is defined by nanoflann's tree build and traversal and which no crate (and no simple (distance, index) tie-break) reproduces: on outline-like data brute force yields the same reported shape pair in only 8,321 of 16,000 queries. Ties are structural there because consecutive outline segments share end points. The hand port reproduces both queries exactly. Prototype: /home/user/kicad-source-mirror/rust/target/research/spatial/src/nanoflann_port.rs.
libs.fidelity_risk: low with the hand port (exact on all tested queries). With brute force or a crate: none for well-formed outlines (radius path is canonicalised by KiCad), medium for malformed outlines (the items named in the "not a closed shape" violation can differ).

It is pulled in by thirdparty/dynamic_bitset/dynamic_bitset.h:59-63 (`__has_include(<libpopcnt.h>)`) and used in exactly one place, `dynamic_bitset::count()` (dynamic_bitset.h:2745-2746), i.e. LSET/BASE_SET::count(). thirdparty/dynamic_bitset/CMakeLists.txt links the `popcnt` interface target.
libs.recommendation: std is enough: `u64::count_ones()` summed over the blocks.
libs.rationale: It is only a faster population count; the result is a plain integer with no room for numerical differences. Rust's count_ones compiles to popcnt/NEON where available and to a bit-trick fallback on wasm32 (or the wasm `i64.popcnt` instruction).

libs.kicad_usage: Included by libs/kimath/src/geometry/shape_poly_set.cpp:47 (SHAPE_POLY_SET::cacheTriangulation, line 3490 onward) and by the 3D ray tracer (out of scope). The triangles feed SHAPE_POLY_SET::Collide (via TRIANGULATION_INDEX / AnyTriangleHit), DRC_RTREE for zones (SH_POLY_SET_TRIANGLE subshapes), CN_ZONE_LAYER in connectivity, and the triangulation is cached in zone fills. Distances to a polygon do not depend on how it is triangulated, but collision LOCATIONS for overlapping shapes are taken from the first intersecting triangle, so the exact triangles (and their order) influence DRC marker positions.

libs.cpp_lib: libstdc++ std::sort / std::partial_sort tie order (implicit dependency of KIRTREE, delaunator and nanoflann; not in thirdparty/)
libs.bundled_version: GCC 13.3 libstdc++ (bits/stl_algo.h, bits/stl_heap.h): introsort with median-of-3 pivot, insertion sort below 16 elements, heapsort fallback at depth 2*floor(log2 n).
libs.kicad_usage: Not a bundled library, but the libraries of this group only become reproducible with it: `std::sort` is unstable and the comparators involved leave ties. Call sites that decide output: packed_rtree.h:264 (Hilbert keys; equal for items with the same bbox centre), dynamic_rtree.h:927 (forced reinsert by distance), :1098-1141 and :1287-1303 (R*-tree split axis sorts), delaunator.cpp:304 (point ids by distance to the seed circumcentre; equal distances are normal on symmetric layouts), nanoflann.hpp RadiusResultSet::sort. The same issue will exist for other KiCad code that sorts with a non-total comparator.
libs.recommendation: port by hand: a small `std_sort` / `std_partial_sort` module in kicad-core, used wherever the C++ calls std::sort with a comparator that is not a total order.
libs.rationale: Rust's `sort_unstable_by` produced the libstdc++ order in only 1,197 of 3,102 test arrays (essentially the tie-free ones), and a stable sort is a different permutation again. A 330-line port of the libstdc++ algorithms reproduces the order exactly. `std::stable_sort` needs no port (the result of a stable sort is unique; use `slice::sort_by`). Prototype: /home/user/kicad-source-mirror/rust/target/research/spatial/src/stdsort.rs. One trap found by the overflow checks: __adjust_heap relies on signed truncating division for len 0 and 1 (std::partial_sort(first, first, last) still moves the minimum to the front), so the port uses isize there.
libs.fidelity_risk: low: exact against the Linux/GCC reference. Inherent caveat: the order of equal elements is libstdc++-specific, so results match a GCC-built oracle but would not match KiCad built with libc++ or MSVC, which already differ from each other in these tie cases.
libs.experiments: cpp/sort_driver.cpp vs src/bin/sort_cmp.rs: 4,602 arrays of (key, original index) sorted by key only - 3,000 random arrays with 1..1e9 distinct keys and sizes 0..5,000, structured inputs (sorted, reversed, organ pipe, sawtooth, pairs, at the 15/16/17/32/33 thresholds up to 10,000), McIlroy antiquicksort adversarial inputs up to 10,000 elements (the port took the heapsort fallback 109 times), and 1,500 std::partial_sort cases. Result: 4,602 identical, 0 different (2,322 of the std::sort cases contain ties). The port is additionally exercised indirectly by every delaunator / r-tree / nanoflann comparison above, natively and in wasm32.
